newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O.LICHT - 3rd estimate of world sugar production.
newsitem.headline: F.O.LICHT - 3rd estimate of world sugar production.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity
statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address
any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.
All figures in 1,000-tonnes, raw value, first figure 1996/97,
second figure 1995/96, figures in brackets previous estimate
World sugar production in 1996/97 is now estimated at 123.3
million tonnes. Though that is some 3.3 million tonnes less than the
initial forecast made in October of last year, prices have
been remarkably resilient during the past half year. Though

The reason that prices apparently do not reflect
statistics is not hard to fathom. The reduction in the
estimate of production is mainly the result of a drop in the

expected crop in India and just as the build up of unsaleable supplies in that country did not affect world market prices last year, so news that the current crop's output will be much lower than originally expected has had no effect this year.

The European Union plays a pivotal role in the white sugar market but for a number of reasons it was expected that output would fall in 1996/97. That was not the case, however, and output is expected to be about 960,000 tonnes higher on the year. The EU Commission has recently published statistics purporting to show the increased outlet there will be for sugar produced in the EU 15 when the first of the new countries adhere to the Community. This may be dangerous and could lead farmers to ignore the problems they may soon have to face. We believe that membership of the EU will lead to an expansion of production in these countries, not the reverse.
Outside the EU, Turkey will have a good crop, not far from our original forecast, and one which will allow the country to be an exporter of white sugar.

In East Europe, the problems of the Ukraine and Russia are well known. Factories are old and are suffering from a lack of cash. Meanwhile Russia has erected a tax barrier against sugar from the Ukraine. Poland has a record crop in 1996/97 but even success in these countries brings its difficulties and the government will insist on lower sowings in 1997 in order to reduce stocks. Despite the higher crop in Poland the overall figure for East Europe was down this year.

Outside Europe production from beet is put at about 7.5 million tonnes or about 190,000 tonnes down on the year. The USA is the largest beet sugar producer and in 1996/97 it reached 3.63 million tonnes, slightly up on output the previous season. In China production reached 1.5 million tonnes which was higher than output the previous year, but a figure that had been exceeded in the past.

At last the cane sector is expecting a setback, though only from 86.9 million tonnes in 1995/96 to 85.4 million tonnes in 1996/97. The big loser this year is Asia where production in India is expected to drop to 14.3 million tonnes from 17.9 million tonnes the previous season. Thailand's regular increases have also come to a halt with 6.1 million tonnes, raw value, expected compared with 6.3 million tonnes in 1995/96. Output in Indonesia is put at 2.1 million tonnes, down from what was produced last year and well below either targets or levels attained in the past. Though the goal of self sufficiency has not been abandoned it now appears to be farther off than ever. Various problems were encountered in Pakistan and it was expected that production would be seriously affected. In the event, however, it was down by only 3.3 per cent. Not long ago the Philippines was one of the world's leading sugar exporters. Those days have gone and the country is now an importer with a shortfall of 370,000 tonnes expected next year. Not all of Asia has done badly, however, China expects to produce around 5.8 million tonnes, which is the best level for some years.

It was thought that Cuba was gradually crawling back towards her previous important position in the sugar market, but various difficulties have been encountered and the Cuban President has hinted that last year's output will not be exceeded. Mexico, on the other hand is expected to reach about 4.8 million tonnes, up 100,000 tonnes on the year. Production in mainland USA is expected to be down by about 140,000 tonnes, but an improvement is looked for in 1997/98.

Brazil will assume top spot this year with 14.7 million tonnes, up about one million tonnes on the year. This puts other producers in South America in the shade though Colombia is expected to reach 2.1 million tonnes and Argentina 1.4 million tonnes.

In Africa the crop in the Republic of South Africa reached 2.4 million tonnes, within striking distance of the output regularly attained before the drought years. In Oceania output Australia continues to set new records while the export potential strides towards the five million tonnes mark.

It is very early days but first indications are that output in 1997/98 will be around 123 million tonnes or not much changed on the year. While production is expected to show little change from 1996/97 offtake will continue to grow and the build up of stocks could come to a halt in 1997/98. With a little bit of luck exporters can even look forward to a modest decline in stocks which should support world prices although much will depend on regional developments.
